title: Confronting over familiarity in stories, do you experience this?

commenti.body:
Part of the problem is there aren't all that many stories out there, really, so if your primary pleasure in movies (or books, or whatever) is the story, you're going to burn out. As you've seen. 

>Of course, the artistry can be found in THE WAY a story is told as well, which is true.

I'd argue that, to the degree that film is a narrative medium (which it isn't always), the way the story is told is the primary source of artistry, not a secondary one. If the story is the most important thing, why are you watching a movie instead of watching a show or reading a book or skimming plot summaries on Wikipedia? 

Not obsessing about the story also means it doesn't matter whether or not you figure out what's going on before the movie makes it explicit.

You can level up as a film lover by letting go of plot and mechanics as the primary reasons to watch a movie. 

Films are so much more than that. There’s enjoyment to be found in the performances, the photography, editing, music, costumes, ambience, artifice, sound design, on and on. It all works in concert to create a unique experience. Some of the greatest films of all time have simple—even predictable!—plots. 

If none of those things interest you, then it’s possible that film simply isn’t your medium. Nothing wrong with that either.

I agree and some of my favorite films actually have no to little plot. I find myself gravitating more and more to abstract, experimental but shorter films. And films that, as we said, with no plot. Something about watching a story about nothing helps alleviate this kind of boredom of waiting I have with more plot driven movies. But soon, I'll get tired of it as well I imagine, especially since those types of films need a certain mindset to experience.

And, really, this problem in watching film I have is also encountered in other forms of media. Besides literature, It's become more difficult to hold my pace with a story knowing the few places it can go. I feel film won't be the medium I can stick with long-term, unless I devote myself to watching old sad movies all day which would drive me crazy

> Part of the problem is there aren't all that many stories out there, really

Exactly so it slowly and surely becomes a kind big stereotype made out of a collection of smaller ones. "If he does that then the possibilities are XYZ and if he chooses X then there's no escaping that the story might go A or B." It becomes a chore unless the film is exceptionally directed and presented in a way that lives beyond its story. The stories that entertainment are the ones that aren't even focused on the story.

I spoke about that in the OP
> Of course, the artistry can be found in THE WAY a story is told as well, which is true. But even the ways a story is told I find to be so mechanical and prepackaged often. If it's one of those artsy dream like films, it'll have disturbing images and some surreal moments and maybe a doppelganger will appear. Maybe the walls of a room will fall down like it's a play, and the characters will spend a few minutes walking around as a single shot, etc. I'm always watching pre prepared and when it comes it is unsurprising

Or, in other words, even how a story is told is beginning to lose its charm save for a few decades, countries, and directors (who hardly work anymore)
I don’t think you understood the comment you responded to

This happens to me a lot. I study movies to improve my novel writing. I write about movies for a living, specifically narrative and thematic deconstructions.

So I get incredibly frustrated by predictability. Sometimes the tropes are fine and I get swept up in the characters, world, etc. Other times, it’s just infuriatingly by the numbers and basic. I often say on our podcast that I just want to not know what’s going to happen next. Keep me on my toes and I’ll be happy. That’s it. 

That’s why something like Barbarian was so refreshing. Or why I love Beau is Afraid way more than Oppenheimer. Interstellar frustrated me because “the main character is the answer to the mystery” was so disappointing. I want to buy-in but as soon as they introduce the “ghost” the most obvious answer is “It’s Cooper.” Lo and behold.

It’s why Hateful Eight and Glass Onion bother me. Their first 60-ish minutes are done in a way that really only works for first-time viewing. Once you know what happens, they lose so much momentum and tension. 

It can become a pretty big problem if pattern recognition leads to boredom. But some people don’t mind. Others actually enjoy it. So it goes.
